adjudication_label: batch_2:BCC/FCC Dual-Phase Microstructure Formation and Segregation
canonical_question: How do temperature-dependent diffusion barriers, simultaneous nucleation-growth mechanisms, and undefined kinetic timescales explain the presence or absence of BCC phases and FCC-to-BCC transformation rates in FeNiCrMn and CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys under mechanical alloying and tensile deformation?

incompatibilities.description: Presence of BCC atoms: One evidence span claims BCC atoms are observed around disordered atoms with increasing temperature, while another explicitly states no BCC atoms were observed in any orientation, indicating no transformation occurred.

question_variants.question: How does the 'reduction in diffusion energy barrier' at higher temperatures quantitatively affect the rate of 'FCC-to-BCC transformation' observed?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text states that higher temperatures reduce the diffusion energy barrier for FCC-to-BCC transformation, but the same text explicitly notes that no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation was observed in the simulations. Therefore, the quantitative effect on the rate of such a transformation cannot be determined because the transformation did not occur in the studied regime.

answers.answer: While higher temperatures reduce the diffusion energy barrier for FCC-to-BCC transformation, no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation was observed in the simulations. Thus, there is no quantitative rate of transformation to report for the observed conditions.
answers.measurement_outcome: No BCC atoms observed; transformation did not occur
answers.mechanism: Barrier reduction exists theoretically but transformation not observed
answers.boundary_limitation: Transformation not observed in the specific experimental/simulation regime
evidence_spans: The primary dislocations observed were Shockley partial dislocations and stair-rod immobile dislocations.
No BCC atoms were observed in any of the three orientations, indicating that no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation occurred during tensile deformation.
The yield strength of the alloy was relatively insensitive to strain rate within the simulated range.

source_evidence_spans: This phenomenon occurs because higher temperatures reduce the diffusion energy barrier for the FCC-to-BCC transformation [ [30] ].

evidence_spans: High–entropy alloy powders composed of CoCrFeNiTi were prepared using a mechanical alloying process through high–energy ball milling (HEBM) under argon atmosphere.

These elemental powders included cobalt (99.8% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), chromium (99.7% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 30 µm), iron (99.96% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 20 µm), nickel (99.5% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), and titanium (99.95% purity, particle ranging from 2 µm to 5 µm).
The milling process was conducted using a planetary ball mill model QM–1SP4, utilizing a stainless steel cylindrical vessel and balls with diameters between 5 mm and 10 mm.

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: There is a consensus that the 'kinetics of alloys' in the specific context of MA/SPS are not thoroughly examined or defined regarding phase transformation rates versus diffusion coefficients [PMC12298864::reader_question::da254d6a61ef969b::answer::ce32680a571f26bb]. Furthermore, the theoretical reduction of diffusion energy barriers at higher temperatures does not guarantee transformation if the specific transformation conditions (e.g., tensile deformation at specific rates) are not met [PMC12029629::reader_question::4c9d7d5e6c8917b6::answer::14d007716e0020db].
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: One study on FeNiCrMn HEA under tensile loading investigates the transformation kinetics via simulations, focusing on diffusion barriers and specific orientations, yet finds no transformation occurred despite theoretical barriers being reduced [PMC12029629::reader_question::4c9d7d5e6c8917b6::answer::14d007716e0020db]. In contrast, studies on CoCrFeNiTi HEA via mechanical alloying focus on the temporal aspect of nucleation, noting an approximate 5-hour nucleation time for FCC and a lack of obvious nucleation time for BCC, attributing the latter to simultaneous nucleation and growth [PMC12298864::reader_question::7aeb419fabe8a5ac::answer::370655a67ae04868, PMC12298864::reader_question::cd2a5be891d23518::answer::7549648ce8b80636].
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The occurrence of BCC phases and the observation of transformation rates are strictly dependent on the processing state (simulated tensile deformation vs. mechanical alloying) and the specific temperature/strain rate regime. In FeNiCrMn, no BCC was observed at 10-600 K under tensile loading [PMC12029629::reader_question::4c9d7d5e6c8917b6::answer::14d007716e0020db], whereas in CoCrFeNiTi, BCC formation is linked to the milling process itself without a distinct nucleation lag [PMC12298864::reader_question::cd2a5be891d23518::answer::7549648ce8b80636].
cross_paper_synthesis.contradictions: A direct contradiction exists within the FeNiCrMn tensile deformation data: one span reports observing BCC atoms around disordered atoms with increasing temperature, while another span explicitly states 'No BCC atoms were observed in any of the three orientations' [PMC12029629::reader_question::d1d17f0a6a23433c::answer::eff919914c7316ca].
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: Evidence for the 'no transformation' conclusion in tensile tests is strong based on explicit negative observations across orientations [PMC12029629::reader_question::4c9d7d5e6c8917b6::answer::14d007716e0020db]. Evidence for 'simultaneous nucleation' in mechanical alloying is observational and linked to the lack of a defined nucleation time point [PMC12298864::reader_question::cd2a5be891d23518::answer::7549648ce8b80636]. The link between sampling resolution and nucleation time definitions is weak due to missing information in the source text [PMC12298864::reader_question::7aeb419fabe8a5ac::answer::370655a67ae04868].
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: It remains unresolved whether the 'reduction in diffusion energy barrier' at higher temperatures quantitatively correlates with transformation rates in any regime, as no transformation was observed in the tensile study [PMC12029629::reader_question::4c9d7d5e6c8917b6::answer::14d007716e0020db]. Additionally, the definition of 'kinetics' (transformation rates vs. diffusion coefficients) remains unspecified in the literature [PMC12298864::reader_question::da254d6a61ef969b::answer::ce32680a571f26bb], and the relationship between the 5-hour nucleation time and sampling intervals is unexplained [PMC12298864::reader_question::7aeb419fabe8a5ac::answer::370655a67ae04868].
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: The BCC phase in mechanical alloying forms via a mechanochemical simultaneous nucleation-growth mechanism that bypasses classical time-dependent nucleation, whereas in tensile deformation, the diffusion energy barrier reduction is insufficient to overcome the critical activation energy required for FCC-to-BCC transformation at the tested strain rates, leading to a stable FCC structure or contradictory detection artifacts.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: Perform in-situ high-energy X-ray diffraction on FeNiCrMn HEA during mechanical alloying (simulating the CoCrFeNiTi conditions) while varying the strain rate to distinguish between simultaneous nucleation (no lag) and thermally activated nucleation (5-hour lag), and simultaneously resolve the contradictory BCC detection in tensile tests by correlating local atomic environments with diffraction patterns.
